newsitem.title: UGANDA: Iran's president arrives in Uganda on Africa tour.
newsitem.headline: Iran's president arrives in Uganda on Africa tour.

text.p: Iranian President Hashemi Rafsanjani arrived in Uganda from Kenya on Thursday on the second leg of a six-nation African tour to drum up business for the Islamic republic.

Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni welcomed Rafsanjani on his arrival at Entebbe airport aboard a Boeing 747. After a 21-gun salute, traditional dancers and a Moslem group of drummers entertained the Iranian president before he left for Kampala.
Rafsanjani arrived from Kenya where on Thursday he held a second and final round of talks with President Daniel arap Moi.

"The two presidents agreed to strengthen and increase the level of cooperation in all fields with particular emphasis on trade and exchange of information on agriculture, tourism, environment, health, transport and culture," a statement said.
After leaving Uganda on Sunday, the Iranian president is due to visit Sudan, South Africa, Zimbabwe and Tanzania.
Diplomats said his African tour was designed to reduce Iran's international isolation and the impact of U.S. sanctions. Washington accuses Iran of sponsoring terrorism, a charge Iran denies.
Thousands of people -- many waving Ugandan and Iranian flags -- lined the road to Kampala to receive the Iranian leader.
Rafsanjani holds talks later on Thursday with Museveni, who took power in 1986 and has helped lead Uganda to economic recovery from near-ruin under dictators Idi Amin and Milton Obote.
Diplomats said as well as ways to improve trade they expected Museveni and Rafsanjani to discuss Uganda's chilly relations with Sudan. Uganda and Sudan accuse each other of backing rebels.
Rafsanjani has said Iran is offering the hand of brotherhood to Africa after its land was raped by Western colonialists.
Rafsanjani, his wife and an 180-strong Iranian delegation accompanying him meet Moslem religious leaders on Friday and the heads of other faiths on Saturday night, Ugandan officials said.
He will also visit Islamic institutions outside Kampala on Friday to join worshippers for the day's main Islamic prayers.

Rafsanjani's African tour comes less than a month after U.S. President Bill Clinton tightened sanctions against Iran. The law penalises non-U.S. firms that invest $40 million or more a year in the oil and gas sectors of Iran or Libya.
Iran has steadily stepped up its diplomatic presence in Africa and tried to boost cultural and religious links with Moslems on the world's poorest continent.
But with the exception of Sudan none of the countries Rafsanjani will visit has a Moslem majority and in most of them Christianity is the main religion.
South Africa has historically relied on Iranian crude oil and Kenya switched some of its oil imports from Saudi Arabia to Iran after Moi's visit to Tehran in 1995.
While in Kenya, Rafsanjani criticised the United States for its cruise missile attacks against Iraq, Iran's western neighbour, but said the Iraqis had provided the pretext.
The United States fired cruise missiles at Iraqi air defence targets on Tuesday and Wednesday in retaliation for Saturday's incursion by Iraqi armed forces into Kurdish areas in northern Iraq.
